solutions.latex:
A.P. is $2,4,6,8,\ldots$ where $a=2$, $d=2$

We have $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)=132$

$\therefore\dfrac{n}{2}(4+2n-2)=132$

$\dfrac{n}{2}(2+2n)=132\quad\therefore n(1+n)=132$

$\therefore n^2+n-132=0$

$(n+12)(n-11)=0\quad\therefore n=-12$ or $n=11$

But $n>0$ $\therefore n=11$, i.e. 11 days.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: correct equation from sum formula; 1: 11 days

solutions.latex:
We have $\log_a x+3\log_a y=1\quad(1)$

$2\log_a x+\log_a y=1\quad(2)$

$2\times(1)$: $2\log_a x+6\log_a y=2\quad(3)$

$(3)-(2)$: $5\log_a y=1\quad\therefore\log_a y=\frac{1}{5}$

So $\log_a x=1-3\log_a y=1-\frac{3}{5}=\frac{2}{5}$

$\therefore\log_a(xy)=\log_a x+\log_a y=\frac{1}{5}+\frac{2}{5}=\frac{3}{5}$

$P(L\text{ gets seat})=\frac{1}{21}\quad\therefore P(L\text{ not get seat})=\frac{20}{21}$

$A=5000(\sin\alpha+\cos\alpha)$

$\therefore\dfrac{dA}{d\alpha}=5000(\cos\alpha-\sin\alpha)$

For stat. points, $\dfrac{dA}{d\alpha}=0$ $\therefore\cos\alpha-\sin\alpha=0$ $\therefore\tan\alpha=1$ $\therefore\alpha=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$

$\dfrac{d^2A}{d\alpha^2}=5000(-\sin\alpha-\cos\alpha)=5000\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)=-5000\sqrt{2}<0$

$\therefore$ maximum area when $\alpha=\frac{\pi}{4}$

Thus max. area $=5000\left(\sin\frac{\pi}{4}+\cos\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=5000\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)=5000\sqrt{2}\,m^2$

solutions.latex:
Since $2f(1-x)+6=2f(-(x-1))+6$, our graph will be $f(x)$ transformed as follows: reflect in $y$-axis; shift right by 1; dilate by factor 2 vertically; shift up by 6.

Hence new vertex is $(2,-4)\to(-1,-2)$

Easiest is just to transform algebraically:

$y=2f(1-x)+6=2\big[(1-x)^2-4(1-x)\big]+6$

$\therefore y=2\big[1-2x+x^2-4+4x\big]+6=2(x^2+2x-3)+6$

$\therefore y=x^2+2x=x(x+2)$

$x$-ints are $0,-2$ & axis is $x=-1$ $\therefore V=(-1,-2)$

\exfigure{377_q30_s1}
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: some useful working; 1: intercept(s); 1: vertex

solutions.latex:
For a region, we need 3 solutions to $\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}=mx$

i.e. 3 solutions to $x=mx^3+mx$

We see $mx^3+(m-1)x=0$

$x\big(mx^2+(m-1)\big)=0$

So one solution will be $x=0$.

For the other 2 solutions we need $x^2=\dfrac{1-m}{m}=\dfrac{1}{m}-1$

i.e. $x=\pm\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{m}-1}$

For 2 solutions, $\dfrac{1}{m}-1>0$ $\therefore\dfrac{1}{m}>1$

$\therefore 0<m<1$ to make a region.

ALT: In $mx^2+(m-1)=0$ we need $\Delta>0$, ie $-4m(m-1)>0$ $\therefore 4m(m-1)<0$ $\therefore 0<m<1$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: correct answer $0<m<1$ (two ticks shown)

Since $y=\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}$ and $y=mx$ are both odd,

$\therefore$ shaded area $=2\times\displaystyle\int_0^{\sqrt{\frac{1}{m}-1}}\left(\frac{x}{x^2+1}-mx\right)dx$

$=2\times\left[\frac{1}{2}\ln|x^2+1|-\frac{mx^2}{2}\right]_0^{\sqrt{\frac{1}{m}-1}}$

$=\ln\left|\frac{1}{m}-1+1\right|-m\left(\frac{1}{m}-1\right)-(\ln 1-0)$

$=\ln\left|\frac{1}{m}\right|+m-1\ u^2$
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: correct integral using symmetry; 1: correct primitive; 1: correct answer

solutions.latex:
Let $f(x)=e^x-1-x$.

Then $f(0)=e^0-1-0=0$

Also, for $x>0$ we have $f'(x)=e^x-1>0$.

So, since $f(0)=0$ and $f(x)$ is increasing for $x\ge 0$, we must have $f(x)\ge 0$ for $x\ge 0$.

i.e. $e^x-1-x\ge 0$

i.e. $e^x\ge 1+x$.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: complete proof (two ticks shown)

solutions.latex:
For $0\le x\le 1$, $x^2\le x$ $\therefore e^{x^2}\le e^x$ (as $e^x$ is an increasing function).

So, from (i), $\therefore 1+x^2\le e^{x^2}\le e^x$

$\therefore\displaystyle\int_0^1(1+x^2)\,dx\le\int_0^1 e^{x^2}\,dx\le\int_0^1 e^x\,dx$

$\therefore\left[x+\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1\le\displaystyle\int_0^1 e^{x^2}\,dx\le\Big[e^x\Big]_0^1$

$\therefore\left(1+\frac{1}{3}\right)-(0-0)\le\displaystyle\int_0^1 e^{x^2}\,dx\le e^1-e^0$

i.e. $\dfrac{4}{3}\le\displaystyle\int_0^1 e^{x^2}\,dx\le e-1<e$, as required.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: $1+x^2\le e^{x^2}\le e^x$; 1: integrates the inequality; 1: evaluates bounds
